{{Short description|American solid state physicist}}
'''Dale J. Van Harlingen''' (July 22, 1950 - July 20, 2024) was an American condensed matter physicist.

==Education and career==
Van Harlingen graduated from [[Ohio State University]] with a bachelor's degree in 1972, a master's degree in 1974 and a doctorate in 1977. As a postdoc he spent a year at the [[Cavendish Laboratory]] in Cambridge, England and three years with [[John Clarke (physicist)|John Clarke]] at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], where he did research on non-equilibrium superconductors and DC electronics with [[SQUID]]s. Van Harlingen became in 1981 a professor at the [[University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign]] (UIUC) and was then a professor of physics at the UIUC's Laboratory for Materials Research and the NSF Science and Technology Center for Superconductivity.<ref name=BuckleyPrize>{{cite web|title=1998 Oliver E. Buckley Condensed Matter Physics Prize Recipient, Dale J. Van Harlingen|website=Dale J. Van Harlingen|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Van%20Harlingen&first_nm=Dale&year=1998}}</ref><ref name=homepage/>

Van Harlingen did research "on the physics of superconductor materials and devices and on the application of microfabrication, cryogenic, and superconductor electronic techniques to problems of fundamental interest in [[condensed matter physics]]."<ref name=BuckleyPrize/> He and his team created innovative scanning probe instruments, especially, the Scanning SQUID Microscope which does imaging of vortex configurations and dynamics in superconductor systems. After [[high-temperature superconductivity]] was discovered in 1986, Van Harlingen and his colleagues pioneered the phase-sensitive SQUID [[interferometry]] technique which enabled the verification of the exotic [[Atomic orbital|d-wave]] symmetry.<ref name=NAS>{{cite web|title=Dale J. Van Harlingen|website=National Academy of Sciences|url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/dale-j-van-harlingen-f5qolc/}}</ref> In fundamental experiments, with [[David Wollman]], [[Donald Ginsberg]] and [[Anthony Leggett]], he determined the symmetry properties of the order parameter in high-temperature superconductors involving some copper oxides.<ref name=BuckleyPrize/> The discovery of such symmetry properties caused a huge research effort to understand the exotic d-wave symmetry and its relation to the mechanisms of unconventional superconductors.<ref name=NAS/>

In 1998 he received, jointly with [[John R. Kirtley]], [[Donald Ginsberg]] and [[Chang C. Tsuei]], the [[Oliver E. Buckley Condensed Matter Prize]] for "using phase-sensitive experiments in the elucidation of the orbital symmetry of the pairing function in high-T<sub>c</sub> superconductors."<ref name=BuckleyPrize/> He was elected in 1995 a fellow of the [[American Physical Society]],<ref>{{cite web|title=APS Fellow Archive|website=American Physical Society|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=1995&unit_id=&institution=University+of+Illinois%2C+Urbana-Champaign}} (search on year=1995 and institution=University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign)</ref> in 1999 a member of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]],<ref name=homepage>{{cite web|title=Dale J Van Harlingen|website=Physics, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign|url=https://physics.illinois.edu/people/directory/profile/dvh}}</ref> and in 2003 a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]],<ref name=NAS/> He was awarded a [[Guggenheim Fellowship]] for the academic year 2001–2002.<ref>{{cite web|title=Dale J. Van Harlingen|website=John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation|url=https://www.gf.org/fellows/all-fellows/dale-j-van-harlingen/}}</ref>
